classification.difficultyReason: Exclude integer roots, then use the supplied quadratic-factor form to constrain and select integer coefficient combinations satisfying all coefficient equations.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that $P(x)$ has no linear factors with integer coefficients.

answer.short: The possible integer roots are $\pm1,\pm2,\pm4$, and none makes $P(x)=0$. Since $P(x)$ is monic, it has no linear factors with integer coefficients.
answer.worked:
Since $P(x)$ is monic, any linear factor with integer coefficients would give an integer root. Test the positive and negative factors of $4$:
$$\begin{align*}P(1)&=-3\\P(-1)&=15\\P(2)&=36\\P(-2)&=12\\P(4)&=540\\P(-4)&=12.\end{align*}$$
None is zero, so the factor theorem rules out every linear factor with integer coefficients.

children.label: b
children.prompt: By writing $P(x)=(x^2+ax+b)(x^2+cx+d)$ and equating coefficients of the expansion, show that $P(x)$ can be factorised to a product of two quadratic polynomials with integer coefficients.

answer.short:
$P(x)=(x^2+2x-4)(x^2+3x-1)$.

Expand the proposed quadratic factors and equate coefficients; $a=2$, $b=-4$, $c=3$, $d=-1$ satisfy all four equations.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}P(x)&=(x^2+ax+b)(x^2+cx+d)\\P(x)&=x^4+(a+c)x^3+(ac+b+d)x^2+(ad+bc)x+bd.\end{align*}$$
Equating coefficients gives
$$\begin{align*}a+c&=5\\ac+b+d&=1\\ad+bc&=-14\\bd&=4.\end{align*}$$
Try $b=-4$ and $d=-1$. Then
$$\begin{align*}a+c&=5\\ac&=6\\-a-4c&=-14.\end{align*}$$
Substituting $a=5-c$ into the last equation gives
$$\begin{align*}-5-3c&=-14\\c&=3\\a&=2.\end{align*}$$
These also satisfy $ac=6$. Hence
$$P(x)=(x^2+2x-4)(x^2+3x-1),$$
a product of two quadratic polynomials with integer coefficients.
